The explanatory remarks will be brief and to the point. I leave this child on the doorstep of the government.

It is not my intention to prevent discussion of this matter, which can be discussed in many other ways, but I must submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. gentleman is not in order in proposing a bill of this kind. This bill deals with government officials, salaries and the expenditure of money, and it is a well known rule of the house that such a bill can be introduced only by a member of the government after receiving the approval of the governor general. Another point that makes it a bill which it is not in order for a private member to introduce is the fact that its adoption would mean the transfer of authority under which appropriated money is to be spent. The salaries of translators have been voted with the estimates of the Secretary of State's department and have been included as such in the appropriation bill. If this bill should carry it would mean that the esti-12739-22$
mates would have to be transferred from one department to several other departments. For both these reasons I submit that this is a money bill that cannot prop.erly be introduced by a private member. I may say, however, speaking to the point, that full opportunity will be given the hon. gentleman and the house to discuss this matter in another form.

Speaking to the point of order, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has said that this is a money bill. What are understood, in the standing orders of this house, by money bills, are bills that contemplate increased expenditure. This bill does not propose one cent more of expenditure; the salaries now paid to the translators will not be changed by this bill. But the control will be different. This is the main point; what we are fighting for is parliamentary control over the officers of this house. It seems most absurd that when, for instance, there are mistakes in the translation of public papers issued by this house, we have to go to a minister of the crown instead of to you, Mr. Speaker, to have the error corrected and the wrong redressed. On the other hand-always speaking to the point of order-I submit that a distinction should be made between a bill involving an increased expenditure of money and a bill that deals with the control of civil servants. In my humble view the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) was wrong when he said that this was a money bill. In fact, there is nothing of that kind contemplated in the bill, everything is left to the governor genera! in council. Personally I am opposed in principle to that form of legislation, but the bill was drafted in that way in order that that very thing should not be complained of. The greater the control we have over the translators the better we follow the general parliamentary rules in force not only here but in all democratic parliaments in the world. Therefore I submit to you that the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, although I regret to say so, is entirely wrong. This is not a money bill and it should be considered on its merits. What I said was not only for the benefit of my colleagues in this house but also for the benefit of the government, because the government is interested in having a better control over the translation work which is done here. I was not surprised at all to see an hon. gentleman on the other side of the house laughing when the matter was brought up, because he has shown a great ignorance of all parliamentary principles since I have been sitting here.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, February 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Heaps:
Whereas there exists in Canada an acute unemployment situation:
And whereas, it is desirable that as many as possible be absorbed into the useful industrial life of the dominion;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government be requested to immediately introduce legislation granting adequate retiring allowances to all_ citizens over sixty years of age, thereby giving an opportunity to large numbers now unemployed to be reabsorbed into useful productive activity.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no wish unnecessarily to prolong the debate on this resolution, first, because I would like to hear the views of the- Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on this resolution-I believe that is what we are waiting for; second, because the next resolution on the order paper is one that I consider to be of great importance. When the house adjourned last night I was pointing out that some of the objections that have been raised against this proposal are absolutely unsound. I pointed out that the argument of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), in endeavouring to wave aside this entire resolution by labelling it state socialism, was 'beside the point. His own leader last year in a radio broadcast made a proposition which in principle was somewhat similar. When I made that statement I noticed the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) shaking his head. I have a great deal of admiration and respect for the right hon. gentleman; and so when he shakes his head I stop and ponder. Consequently I looked up the second of his radio broadcasts, and on page 16 I found these words:
There is another time in the worker's life which must not be forgotten; that time is when, because of old age, he is no longer able to work. As a citizen, he should have security.

It should be a normal and essential function of the state to see that its people, who have contributed to the productivity of the state, who have given their best to the support of the industrial machine, who have spent their vigorous manhood in labour, are not in want when their working days are over.
In the next sentence the prime minister of that time points out wherein he differs from the resolution. He says:
This system of insurance should be on the same social and economic principle as that of unemployment insurance, involving the recognition of thrift on the part of those who will provide for their old age. The present Old Age Pensions Act is unscientific and obsolete and must give way to something which will serve you better.
I do not read that because I wish to tie the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) up to this resolution but because I want to point out to the hon. member for Broadview that while in detail it is not the same, in principle it is the same; that it is simply beside the point to try to wave away this important matter by labelling the whole thing state socialism.
Then the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) tried to wave this proposal aside by attacking the underlying philosophy of the motion and saying that this was an age of scarcity rather than an age of abundance. I had understood, sir, that there were antediluvians who still believed in an age of scarcity, but I hardly expected to find them in the House of Commons. I am not prepared to go into a lengthy discussion of this matter because it is irrelevant, but in this day and age it is hardly necessary to point out to any group of individuals the fact that in every line of industry the power to produce has progressed tremendously even in the last ten years. The hon. member for Melfort based his assumption on a statement made by a well known Swedish economist, to the effect that in 1928 production and consumption were running very close together. But it should be remembered that he referred to effective consumption, and we know that effective consumption was possible only because of instalment buying and the mortgaging of the future; that even in 1928 it was very difficult to distribute sufficient purchasing power to consume the large quantities produced. But here is the remarkable fact, that even since 1928 we have gone a long way. In a recent radio speech the President of the United States pointed out that if we could return industry to its peak of 1928 there would still be in the United States six million men who would find no employment because their places had been taken by machines. In

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Douglas
other words we have progressed so far that in 1936 we are able to produce as much as we produced in 1928 without the services of six million men who were employed at that time.

speechtext:
In the United States, but the same principle applies here. In all the world to-day there are more than thirty million men who are unemployed, yet we are able to feed the people of the world and keep them up to some standard of living, which is adequate proof of the fact that we are producing far more than we produced a generation ago.
The hon. member for Melfort also attacks this resolution on the ground that the whole difficulty in Canada to-day is the fact that providence has not wept. After listening to a statement like that I think providence ought to weep. May I point out that providence wept in Ontario, providence wept in the British Isles and in France, Germany, Italy and Japan. Providence wept in other places, but in spite of that fact they had an economic crisis. If the entire problem that we are facing is due to the fact that we have had no crops and that this is an age of scarcity, then, Mr. Speaker, in Canada to-day we should have a shortage of wheat. Instead of that, however, the government is wrestling with a surplus of over 200,000,000 bushels, and if the crops had been normal for the last five years the surplus -would be nearer 800,000,000 bushels. Therefore I think the attack upon the underlying philosophy is simply an attempt to throw up a smoke screen in connection with this matter.
I do think, however, that the argument advanced by the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Deachman) is one about which we ought to think. It brings up the problem of finding money, and that is something that will interest the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), as it ought to interest every member of this house. It is a remarkable thing that whenever one brings up legislation involving the welfare and happiness of the people of Canada, someone wants to know where the money is coming from, yet in this country we find money for a great many other things. In the Dominion of Canada we have a governmental service and governmental machinery that is preponderantly heavy. One prominent United States social scientist said to me in Chicago university some time ago, "In Canada you have enough government machinery to run Canada and the United States put together." In addition we have innumerable commissions, a great many of which-or so it would seem to the
public at least-are designed to provide jobs for people who are supposed to deserve their reward. It is costing the people of Canada millions of dollars every year to provide comfortable pasturage for worn out political war horses who have entered upon their reward. We also have a judicial system that has become heavy and complex, that overlaps and is expensive, yet no one asks where the money is to come from for that. In Canada we pay millions upon millions of dollars in interest on bonds. Much of that money was invested when money was cheap, but the interest is being collected to-day when money is dear, when the purchasing power of that money is much greater. Yet we keep on paying those interest charges and no one asks where the money is to come from. The other day we voted an estimate of almost $2,000,000 to look after the health of the cattle of Canada. No one asked where the money was coming from, but when we come to talk about looking after the old people someone wants to know where we are to get the money.
I want to suggest that in my estimation there are three ways by which money could be secured for this purpose. On looking over the past records I find that in 1931 some
63,000	people were receiving old age pensions, costing the country about $14,000,000. In 1935 that number had increased to 82,000 persons, which cost the country some $16,000,000. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a paltry sum compared to the service that is rendered, and compared to the huge sums of money that we spend elsewhere for services that are far less valuable to the people of Canada. I submit that we might find money first of all by curtailing certain expenditures, certain appointments and certain commissions; by reshaping our whole governmental policy in order to cut down duplication; by refunding or reconverting some of our loans at lower interest rates, and collecting income tax on government bonds. I believe in these ways sufficient money could be raised to meet the cost of this undertaking. It might even be possible that the Minister of Finance would be prepared to go so far as to institute, through the Bank of Canada, a national credit fund by which we would be prepared to issue credit against the security of the Dominion of Canada. If it is possible for the government to issue credit against government bonds deposited by financial institutions it should be possible for the government of Canada to issue its own credit against the security of the people of Canada. Of course the cry im-
Retiring Allowances-Mr. Douglas

mediately is "inflation," yet I need hardly remind hon. members that the most orthodox economists admit that the quantity theory of money shows that inflation takes place only when money is issued in excess of goods produced. For the last five years we have had deflation, very rapid deflation, the withdrawal of currency and credit coincident with increase of goods produced, the result being that the relationship between money and goods is out of balance. It would be possible to-day to set up a very large national credit account without in any way upsetting the proper relationship between currency, credit and goods produced.
I ask, therefore, that the house give to this resolution its most urgent attention. We support it not because we wish to place the government on the spot, not because we wish to stick on this detail or that, but because we know that all across Canada to-day there are thousands of men who have been replaced by younger men, salesmen, for instance, who five years ago were receiving fair incomes but whose places have been taken by young university graduates. Two months ago I stood in a foundry in Winnipeg among men who work beside a great electric furnace with a temperature of 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit, men who have served their day and generation, and who at sixty years of age are prematurely worn out. We heard of one man who after thirty-four years of service was told he was no longer required. His work had never been steady; it had been seasonal; every winter some men were laid off for at least part of the time. They had never been able to lay aside any large amount of money, and in the case of this man the result was that it meant resorting to public charity for himself and his wife. I ask hon. members most earnestly to give this resolution sober and thoughtful consideration, keeping in mind the men and women to whom Canada owes a debt. Let us do our best to see their need and meet their problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me extend to you my humble congratulations on your elevation to your present position. The first time I haul the opportunity of observing the deliberations of the House of Commons it was under the speakership of the Hon. Mr. Lemieux, and at that time I was filled with admiration at the wonderful way in which he presided over the house. Since the opening of this parliament I have watched the manner in which you, sir, have presided over our deliberations, and in my opinion you have attained fully

to the ideal and worthily followed the traditions honoured in this house by the Hon. Mr. Lemieux.
I do not need to tell hon. members, especially those who have sat in this house before and have gone through the experience of rising in this chamber for the first time, how nervous I feel and with what diffidence, Mr. Speaker, I address the house through you. As I look back over Canadian history and consider the great men who have sat in this House of Commons since 1867; as I have read from time to time the speeches of those who led both the great historic parties from confederation to recent times, and as I consider those who to-day are leading all parties in this house, their patriotism, their devotion to public affairs, I am satisfied that never before have we had men more capable and more devoted to the best interests of the people. So it is with diffidence and humility and deference that I rise to advance any ideas before this house. Each of us, however, has an obligation to express his opinions and to voice the wishes of the constituents by whom he was sent here.
As I consider this motion I am satisfied I should not be doing my duty to my constituents did I not express in this house my unqualified support of the resolution-with this exception, that it calls for immediate legislative action. I quite realize, sir, that the question where the money is to come from cannot be left out of consideration. The government must have time to adopt policies which will enable them to provide the money before we can expect them to bring in such legislation. That is only responsible government. I will deal with that in a moment, but here I should like to say that as far as old age pensions are concerned, if there is anything that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has done that above all else has earned the grateful thanks of large numbers of people it is the legislation that he introduced providing for old age .pensions. Furthermore, the country has not overlooked those who supported that legislation, no matter in what part of the house they sat. Many old people have had the evening of their lives made happier by their action, and above all by the leadership in that regard of the Prime Minister. When the time comes that the Prime Minister finishes his work, one of the outstanding things for which he will be remembered in history will be the fact that he took one of the first steps to make things a little more economically secure for people who were unable to look after themselves.

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Tucker
Something was said in the course of this debate of which I desire to express my disapproval. It was suggested that one reason the party of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was not successful in the last election was that he expressed the idea that something of this sort should be done in Canada, that the people of Canada expressed their dissent from that view by not returning him to power. I suggest that the Conservative party was defeated not because he expressed that idea, but for other reasons, and in spite of his having taken that stand. I believe that the majority of the people of Canada expect this parliament to take steps to restore economic security to people who are unable to look after themselves owing to economic conditions over which they have no control.
As I see it, this resolution has to do with three types of people. First there are the old people between sixty and seventy who by reason of being physically unfit cannot get a job to enable them to look after themselves. I submit it is our duty to look after those who are unable to take care of themselves. If there is one thing that Christian society has recognized as its paramount duty ever since there has been Christian society it is that of looking after those who cannot look after themselves. I submit that the time is coming nearer and nearer when we shall refuse to leave those people to be looked after by charity, and shall recognize that we must use the resources of the state to care for them. That applies to returned soldiers who are now unable to eam a living. It certainly applies to those who are afflicted with blindness and cannot provide for themselves. As far as I am concerned I shall not be satisfied if before its life is over this parliament shall not have taken some real steps that will cause it to go down in history as having done more to this end than any parliament that has preceded it.
There is another category of people to whom the resolution would apply, namely those doing casual work, people who are eking out some kind of existence by competing in a precarious sort of way in the labour market, people who are preventing younger men and women from obtaining work. Although we do not know just what proportion of the total they constitute, we do know that many of them would gladly accept $20 a month rather than have to go on living partly through the charity of friends and partly through smashing down wages to a level at which a young man cannot possibly work and earn a living for himself and family. When we extend to those people the benefits of a measure such as the one before us, we are achieving two objects: first, we are looking
after people who have served the state faithfully and well for a period of possibly forty years; and second, we are furnishing a large measure of employment.
As in a humble sort of way I have studied public affairs for many years and have read about people who have been fortunate enough to obtain government positions, people who, having served the government for a certain number of years, eventually have arrived at the age of superannuation, and as I read about ordinary government employees being superannuated at $3,000 a year, my mind goes back to the pioneers who settled the country. I think of the people, for example, who went out to western Canada, men who, taking their wives with them, settled miles and miles away from medical assistance. They took the very lives of their children in their hands when they went to those areas. They worked and slaved for years and years. They did the work of the nation, because they were growing the food of the nation. When I consider that we say to those people that we cannot give them even $20 a month but that we can give $200 or $300 a month to people who have been more fortunate because they have secured government jobs, and did not have to face those vicissitudes, I am convinced that it is not fair. In doing that I submit we are giving less than justice to the people who settled the country, and endured great dangers and privations in doing so. We must do something more than simply dismiss their claim; we cannot be content with saying that we have not the money.
There is another category of people who would be affected, namely those between the years of sixty and seventy who are well able to make a living for themselves, who have no desire for this legislation, and whom, I understand, the legislation as explained by the proposer would not affect. With considerable hesitation I suggest that there is growing up in Canada among our young people a feeling that the older people are prepared to hang on to their jobs, even when they have reached eighty years, thereby keeping their grandchildren on the bread line, and in a position where they cannot get married and establish homes for themselves. In other words they are beginning to feel that their fathers and grandfathers are not treating them as if they were of their own flesh and blood. As the average longevity is increasing, due to the advance of medical science, we must give consideration to this problem. If a man who has reached the age of seventy-five years and has made a real contribution to the society of his day and age continues to hold his position for another ten years, he is thereby

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Tucker
depriving some other man of the dearest thing in the world, namely the chance to make his contribution to his day and age. As the resolution does not suggest any solution for this condition I say we should do something about it. One could not reach any conclusion in the matter without first giving it a great deal of serious thought and consideration. It is a fact however that the circumstance I have indicated is in the minds of our young people.
One now comes to a consideration of the cost of a pension scheme. According to the Canada Year Book there are 525,731 males and females in Canada between the ages of sixty and seventy. Assuming half those people were paid $20 a month, the cost in round figures would amount to $63,000,000. Suppose half the applicants for pension were able to compete on the labour market-and that is putting it at a very high figure-and that that half were given a pension, thereby leaving only a half of the total number to deprive others of work, we would provide jobs for 131,000 young people.
As the relief camp at Dundum is in the constituency of Rosthern, which I have the honour to represent in this house, I am keenly interested in the young men in the relief camps. I realize that I represent those boys at Dundum camp; I have visited them, and believe I know something of the attitude of the young people in Canada. I know what they expect; I believe they expect some real, wholesale measure of relief, and they will not be satisfied with any nibbling. They want jobs-lots of jobs. As I have indicated, the measure before us could be made to provide jobs for 131,000 young people. That would be worth while, and the people of Canada would be in a position to say, " Well, at least this parliament is doing something to justify its existence; they are not talking, and doing nothing else."
I do not intend to discuss the cost at great length, but I shall lay only a few facts before hon. members for their careful consideration. Although the facts I am about to detail are not new, I feel it my duty to state them. I do so without a chip on my shoulder; I do it in all humility and for the sake of the future of Canada.
First, I hear the statement on every hand that our public debt is due to the war. That is a popular suggestion. My figures, which I suggest are reliable and worthy of consideration, are taken from the report of the royal commission on banking and currency which sat in 1933 and reported to this chamber. According to the report I find that in 1914 the total debt in Canada, dominion,

provincial, municipal and public corporate debt-that is, the debt of us as a people, not including our private debts-was $2,232,000,000. In 1919 it had risen to $3,749,000,000, an increase of approximately $1,500,000,000. I was surprised, however, when I read that in 1929 the debt had risen to $7,445,000,000. In other words during a period of real prosperity in the ten years between 1919 and 1929 it had increased to twice as much as it had been immediately following the war.' What have those people to say who urge that our debt is due to the war. I find that by 1932 the debt had risen to $8,652,000,000. What does that mean? It simply means that from 1919 to 1932 the public debt of this country increased by more than one million dollars a day. And that was happening all over the world. We are told that that debt increased because people were saving up money and lending it out. I would like to know where the wealthy people are in Canada who have been saving a million dollars a day to lend to the government outside of what they lend to private corporations. I shall show, Mr. Speaker, that when the banks lend money they do not lend solely the savings of the people. It is true they lend the savings of the people, but they lend also credit which they themselves create.

Now if it is all right for the Bank of Montreal to take government bonds, if it is all right for the banks to take $48,000,000 worth of government bonds and obtain new money against those bonds, then it should be all right for the Bank of Canada to advance whatever money this country needs against dominion, municipal and provincial government bonds. To-day, as I understand the Bank of Canada Act, the Bank of Canada will give credit in its books, dollar for dollar, against dominion government bonds. What should be done when the time comes that this country needs more credit and there has not been enough credit saved up to finance the government, as happened during the war? The credit of the country was extended and extended. Suppose we need to borrow some money; what happens? Suppose there is not enough saved up-and there will not be enough saved up to finance us if we continue the way we are going. We shall have to go through this process. The banks will want to buy some dominion government bonds. They

will take some of their present bonds to the Bank of Canada and get credit against those bonds, dollar for dollar; and on the strength of that credit they will be able to turn round and buy nine times as many bonds as they deposited in the first place. What has happened? We have used our credit and in effect we are paying interest on it at the rate of probably 30 per cent.
Is it any wonder that we have no money to take care of old people? Is it any wonder we have no money to look after the unemployed? Hon. members of this house will have to consider this question: Are they going to sacrifice the future development of this country, are they going to sacrifice the unemployed, the old and the sick, are they going to neglect to do the things which a civilized country ought to do, in order to be able to pay interest on a basis such as that? That is the question that must be settled. If the present financial system is cramping us, if it has this country in a strait jacket, which is more important-the financial system or the people? I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is up to this parliament to remove that financial strait jacket; it is the duty of this parliament to explore new avenues. I know that there are some people-the Minister of Finance is in that class-who takes the attitude that the suggestion I make is not feasible. Well, I say to him, let us have a trial of it. The present system is not working so satisfactorily that everyone should be ready to die fighting for it, and if some other method is advanced by great thinkers, why can we not at least have a trial of it? And if it works, let us extend it; if it does not work we can abandon it.
In that connection I would remind the house of what was done by the government led by the leader of the opposition; we have not forgotten it. The leader of the opposition will probably find fault with the way in which I am putting it, but in essence this is what was done. They took to the banks $35,000,000 worth of treasury bills of this country, $35,000,000 of obligations of this country, bearing interest at, I believe, 4 per cent. They said to the banks, "We want you to advance us $35,000,000 worth of credit against these obligations of ours, and you shall take these obligations to the Minister of Finance and he will issue against them $35,000,000 worth of new money on which he will charge you 3 per cent." In other words, we borrowed in that way $35,000,000 worth of credit which cost us only one per cent, and I submit that it should not have cost us a cent if we had set up our own central bank and financed that business for ourselves.

As regards the expansion of credit, some people seem to think that if you work through the banks it is not inflation, but that if the country did it through its own banking institution it would be. I could read excerpts from both these reports which indicate this, that when the banks create credit and lend it against government bonds or deposits available to be checked out, they are creating the equivalent of currency just as much as if they had printed it, because more than ninety per cent of the business of this country to-day is done by cheques on deposit accounts. In other words we turn over to the banks ninety per cent of the control over the purchasing power of this country. They have the right to say how much money the people shall have to purchase with. If the banks do it, it is just as much inflation as though the government turned on the printing presses-just as much and no more. In that connection I would like to read from the Financial World of New York one or two paragraphs, which I found in the Magazine Digest, and which illustrate better than any words of mine what I would like to say:
In a democratic capitalistic country like the United States some 90 per cent of the total
business is done through the medium of net demand deposits in banks. Actual currency is used to but a moderate degree. Therefore, if there is to be a great recovery movement, there is required as a base (1) a large volume of net demand deposits and (2) the will to use them.
In times past great changes in the volume of net demand deposits have been due to expansion and contraction of bank credit. In other words, during periods of rising optimum banks have been prone to expand loans and with each loan expansion create a deposit. In this instance, however, we are witnessing the greatest and fastest expansion in net demand deposits in the history of this country with practically no contribution from the banks.
I would like hon. members to note this:
The 1919 boom was financed with a peak of less than 14 billion dollars of net demand deposits. These dropped to around 10 billion dollars in the sprinsr of 1933. On October 30, 1935, they totalled $16,657,000,000.
That is a rise from the peak of over two billion dollars.

I am glad to have this opportunity to speak for the first time in the House of Commons. I have been rather struck with the procedure followed here, the things that are done and the things not done. It appears that every question brought up on the floor of this house revolves around one outstanding point, and that until such time as we can get beyond the framework of the present financial system it is

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Poole
useless to speak of extending social services; for unfortunately we have uplifted the question of finance and have submerged human rights.
I have listened with some interest to the discussion of unemployment relief. I can quite appreciate why many hon. members may not understand the depth of the poverty that exists in this country, because it is seldom one sees poverty on parliament hill. But if you go into the highways and byways of the west you will find to-day both old and young living in poverty, not because they are old, not because they are inefficient, but because governments refuse to recognize their responsibility by doing away with financial monopoly. Why should there be any debate on the question of old age pensions? Is there any man who has scratched below the economic surface who does not recognize that there are thousands of people who are physically and mentally below par and cannot be absorbed into the industrial life of the country because the field is narrowing and industry is choosing only the best? It is the duty of the government to make available the natural resources of the nation to aid those who have passed the age of sixty years. But again we are told, "It cannot be done; we have not the money and we cannot tax," and the question is asked over and over, "Where is the money to come from"? I believe that the members in this corner of the house can well answer that question. I know there are those in this house who smile at the new economics, who have grown up with the traditional outlook, but if you want to know where the money is to come from to do these things, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) gave the answer when he said: You can make it just the same as the bankers make it. But unfortunately most hon. members in this house do not understand the functions of money. If the people of Canada understood the functions of money, its purpose and how it is brought into being, I am convinced that this monetary system would have been changed long ago. I have in mind the message of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the night of the election; it carries some hope. He said:
In the new era which dawns to-day the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and' misery, are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to banish from our land.
But "where is the money coming from"? The first duty of this government is to take from those who have the control of money and place it back in the hands of the state,

and to provide, not only for people who have reached sixty years of age but for every human being in the Dominion of Canada, economic security. Then hon. members may ask: What will you base your money on? Exactly the same as the bankers base theirs on; first, the natural resources of the nation; second, the ability of the people to produce, and third, the natural demand for goods for consumption. The only purpose of money is to distribute goods.

Therefore I come to my proposal. In my opinion and in the opinion of my colleagues, the first step to be taken by way of a permanent solution of this problem is to remove from the labour market all those workers who have reached the age where, especially under conditions of to-day, the worker's social interest, the state's economic interest, equally sugest the wisdom of retirement.
It is, of course, clear to all of us that the old rules governing hours of labour and years of labour can no longer apply, because we live in changed economic conditions. That fundamental truth forces gundamental changes in our whole economic system. These changes embrace changes in conditions of work, hours of work. They also embrace changes in the age of retirement from work.
This new economic trend has already influenced the retirement schemes of certain private enterprises. And these enterprises, after careful estimate of all the factors involved, have met the new conditions by determining upon a retirement age of sixty years.

I know of half a dozen cases that have come to my immediate attention in which officials, having attained that age, have been retired compulsorily, but having paid in to the pension fund they are receiving in many cases the maximum they would receive if they remained on, and their places have been taken by younger men. That is true in many institutions. [DOT]
I will give the house the other side of the picture. The other day when I was in Calgary a man and his wife came to see me; she was sixty-six and he was sixty-eight. So far as I know he never in his life received as much as $1,800 a year. I think that is too high a figure, judging from inquiries which I made. They had brought up a family, bought a small house or two, and had saved during the period of his employment, and they asked me to be the medium of communication by which the sum of $11,400 in cash was paid to the government to secure for them on their joint lives an annuity of $1,000 per annum. That indicates what may be done under one set of conditions.
A few days later another man came to see me, a man whom I knew rather well, who had been in the same employment as the
364	COMMONS
Retiring Allowances-Mr. Bennett
first man. He had reached the age of sixty-eight. He had been retired from work; he received no pension, and he told me that all he had between himself and absolute privation was $200. He told me why he was in that condition. He had been receiving substantially the same wages as the first man, but almost every year sickness had dogged him and his family. An operation here, an illness there, a child laid aside for months, and at the end of his period of work with the corporation that had employed him. retiring without any pension, he had been able to save only $200. He had a little real estate which he had obtained by purchases in buoyant days, but I think probably the city is now the owner of it for taxes.
Those are illustrations of two sets of conditions which have to be considered. I am not going to elaborate upon them this afternoon. I had, before making that statement last year, prepared a definite plan for dealing with this matter. That is not of importance now, because it is no longer possible for me to give effect to it. However I do believe a contributory system of pensions should be enforced in Canada. I believe every man, beginning at a fixed age, should make such a contribution, and I had prepared a plan whereby a person would be able to obtain stamps at every post office, such stamps to be placed in a book. At the end of a given period of time, whether it be sixty or sixty-five years, or whatever period might be agreed upon, the annuity thus earned by the savings of the citizen, with interest computed as we now have it, at the high rate of four per cent, would determine the extent to which pension would be received. I had proposed that the state would bear the cost of administration, and certain other features that need not now be discussed, because there were certain actuarial figures which were not complete. However I do not think it fair to ask the state to bear the entire burden, looking to the long future. There is a lag, which must be taken care of. Some hon. members will recall the speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer in England when introducing a consolidated measure for social relief involving what is now called the dole. That term is applied erroneously in some instances, because it is a sum payable to individuals for which they themselves have made provision-they making a contribution, the employer making a contribution and the state making a contribution. It is a payment, not by the state covering the whole sum, but by three parties, namely, the state, the insured or the individual who

is to receive the benefits, and the employer. That of course applies only to industry or, in the broader sense, to where there is a relationship between employer and employee. But where the relationship between employer and employee does not exist, and it is one merely of a citizen to the state, it does appear to me to be reasonably clear-and I am told that the proposals I had prepared 'were sound -that the citizen and the state together would commence, early in the life of the citizen, savings of amounts which at a given age would enable him or her to receive just what his or her savings amounted to. This should extend alike to farmers' sons and daughters, and to everyone. Everyone should be given the widest possible opportunity to avail himself of the provisions of the proposals which I had formulated.
This proposal contemplates the state paying the whole amount, and that it should be payable to everyone. I ask the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) whether he has given any consideration to the effect that would have upon the character of the people of Canada. I mention that merely in passing, because after all we know that all these social measures-and it has been the experience of all countries-have a profound effect in, shall I say, creating national character. The first social insurance measure on a large scale of which we have any ready knowledge, that of Bismarck in Germany, it will be recalled was a contributory scheme. In other parts of the world the same is true. This is a proposal to have a pension paid without regard to any contribution being made by any party other than the state, and regardless of any consideration other than those of age and want, and, in fact, as the resolution reads it does not even include want.

speechtext: May I ask whether judges make any contribution to their pension, and whether that has a very serious effect upon them?

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member has mentioned judges, for this reason: It is part of the contract by which men abandon large practices, from which they have been receiving large compensation, usually amounting to many times the salaries they are paid, that at the end of a given time they shall receive certain benefits by way of superannuation or pension. They make a contribution that is far greater than that. For instance in the legal profession there is a tradition which has prevailed for a long while in Great Britain, and I am sorry to say to a lesser extent in Canada, that the leaders of the

Retiring Allowances-Mr. Bennett
profession should not more than once refuse the request of the Lord Chancellor to abandon a highly lucrative practice and accept a small salary to serve in judicial positions, it being part of the contract between the state and the man who accepts a seat on the bench that he shall receive certain benefits at the expiration of fifteen years or upon the attainment of a given age.
If hon. members would look at law reports of recent date they would find that men have been appointed to the bench, at least one of whom I know was making not less than from $175,000 to $250,000 per annum and who is now receiving the sum of only $40,000, because he felt it was part of the great tradition of his profession and his duty to abandon his private practice for the purpose of rendering service to the state as a judge. Part of the contract was that without payment of any part of the premium he was to receive from the state a pension to the extent I have indicated. Of course that is not the rule in Canada to the same degree. Nevertheless in this country there are cases where men have abandoned lucrative positions, in which they have been receiving a very large annual compensation, to serve the state for a much smaller sum, on condition that in their old age, when they are no longer fit for service, they may receive the compensation I have mentioned. They have made a distinct contribution, a very distinct one, for the purpose of obtaining a pension.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman not say that people who have worked hard and long in almost any walk of life have made a proper contribution? Is it not merely the contract that is absent, and would not the passing of legislation contemplated by the resolution constitute a contract through which, if they had worked faithfully, at the end of a certain period they would receive security in their old age?

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
I would answer the hon. member in this way: He contemplates their working faithfully, but under the working of the resolution there is no incentive to work faithfully or unfaithfully. All they have to do is to attain the age mentioned in the resolution, and they will get the money. That is the reason I suggest to the hon. member and to people within sound of my voice that the effect upon the national character of this country would be so apparent within at 'least the life of one generation as to make it extremely difficult to forecast the ultimate result.
Then, there is one other matter I should like to touch upon. I have heard several hon. members say that the age at which pension could be received should be sixty or sixty-five years, or something like that. One of the difficulties in connection with old age pensions has been this: It must be within the knowledge of everyone that fundamentally the question is one within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and that to overcome the difficulty of jurisdiction contributions are made by the dominion under the terms of agreements made between the dominion and the provinces. The pension is paid by the province, not by the dominion. It is amazing to hear some hon. members speak as though the pension were paid by the dominion. The pension is in fact paid and distributed by the provinces. They become responsible for all investigations preceding payment, and although the awarding of the pension is subject to investigation by federal authorities, it is an act of the provincial and not of the federal authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext: It must be so.

The general view is that it must be, although I think there is some doubt as to that. The provinces were originally assisted to the extent of fifty per cent, and under the late administration the amount was increased to seventy-five per cent, and it would have been increased to the whole one hundred per cent if the financial position of the country would have warranted any such action being taken. The time has come, Mr. Speaker, when it is desirable in the interests of Canada that the' government should give very careful consideration and attention to the question of a broad national pension system. I have very strong views upon the subject. I think such a system is feasible. It must be a system that is contributed to by every man who will seek the benefits of it. I would go further and say that if we are going to do anything to develop the character of our people, we should provide that in the event of such contribution not being made by any citizen, he would not have any claim upon the state for relief or other purposes under certain ' conditions that need not be gone into now because they are matters of detail. But the essential fact is that if we had a system based upon a broad national appreciation of our situation-and our numbers are only between ten and eleven million people-we would be aible to provide against the contingencies to which attention has been directed this afternoon and yesterday. In Great Britain, with a population of forty
366	COMMONS
Retiring Allowances-Mr. Bennett
million, they deal with this problem in a national sense; also in Germany, with a population of many more than forty million, perhaps sixty million at least, they do the same.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext: Sixty-seven million.

subtopic: PROPOSED ALLOWANCES AT AGE SIXTY AND OVER
speechtext:
Sixty-seven million, my hon. friend suggests. Germany deals with it in a national way, and the cost of administration has not become so great as to make it burdensome upon the people.
There is just one other thought that should be mentioned, and that is this: How to keep national pensions out of politics has been a matter that has engaged the attention of statesmen of older countries ever since these pensions were begun. There was an election conducted in one country upon the sole, simple issue whether the age for pensions should be reduced by five years; and without any regard for the actuarial facts, without any regard for the effect upon the finances of the country, the election was conducted on that issue. I am bound to say that there are always more people ready and willing to accept benefits than there are willing to pay for them, and the result was, of course, that the lower age carried, but unfortunately the finances did not warrant the providing of the money, and so for the moment they were not any better off than they were at the start.
I did not rise, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of doing more than clarifying the situation to which reference has been made during the present debate. I appreciate the speech of [DOT]the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). I have been compelled myself to make such a speech and I recall that in the position which I then took I had not the support of those who then sat to the left of the Speaker. Now it is some consolation to realize that those responsible for the formulation of government policy-

speechtext:
I had about concluded what I desired to say at this time, except to point out that in addition to the objection that was made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) as to the resolution being in order, there is another point to which I had not expected that it would be necessary to direct attention, but in view of present indications I think it is desirable to do so. This resolution is not within the competence of parliament so far as giving effect to it is concerned. If adopted by parliament, it would be futile because it lies within the powers of the provinces in dealing with property and civil rights-a matter that must be known to most hon. members on this side of the house in view of the opinions that have been given from time to time by the law officers of the crown. I had not intended to raise that issue, but inasmuch as the discussion has assumed the character it has, I think it may be desirable to point that out.
The resolution consists of two preambles and a conclusion. Preamble number one relates to the unemployment situation. Preamble number two says:
And whereas, it is desirable that as many as possible be absorbed into the useful industrial life of the dominion.
That is, the resolution by the preamble deals only with the industrial life of the country. The operative part reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government be requested to immediately introduce legislation granting adequate retiring allowances to all citizens over sixty years of age, thereby giving an opportunity to large numbers now unemployed to be reabsorbed into useful productive activity.
It will be observed that the government is requested by this resolution, if it is passed, to immediately introduce legislation. It is
36S	COMMONS
Retiring Allowances-Mr. Bennett
an expression of the opinion of the house, not that the matter might be considered, but that the government should immediately introduce legislation. To immediately introduce legislation of the character indicated by the resolution would be to introduce legislation beyond the legislative competence of parliament, beyond its jurisdiction. Therefore I submit that the motion is out of order on that ground also.
Apart from that I desire briefly to point out contradictions between the preamble and the operative part of the motion, to which some reference has been made. It is desirable to absorb into the useful industrial life of the dominion as many as possible. To accomplish that end, allowances are to be granted to all citizens over sixty years of age; and the character of the retiring allowances is described as adequate. Adequate to what? Adequate to their present salaries, or compensation-to use the word I suggested this afternoon-or how otherwise? I do not know. But at any rate opportunity is to be given to large numbers now unemployed to be reabsorbed, not into industry, as pointed out in the first preamble, but into useful productive activity. I am not going to do more than say again what I said this afternoon, that if the resolution were to be adopted as it stands now the government would have either to introduce legislation or to resign. If it introduced legislation, that legislation would be futile, because it is beyond our legislative competence, and I think the rules of the house provide that parliament should not be asked to adopt a resolution that is beyond our power to pass. So far as that is concerned I will leave it at that.
There was one point, upon which I was interrupted this afternoon, that I should like to make clear. I pointed out that in my judgment this had to do with a large measure of social reform, and that whenever that measure is adopted by the house, as some day it	will have	to	be,	it will bealong the lines I suggested, by contribution being made by all parties, the state, the employer and the employee in cases where the relationship of employer and employee exists, and by the state and the insured, if you will, or the annuitant, or the pensioner, if you may describe him as such, in other cases. But there will be	a lag of	those whocannot avail	themselves	of	any	such provision. The	Chancellor	of	the	Exchequer,
when social legislation was being considered in England, pointed out that they have to make a yearly grant to take care of that situation, and that yearly grant represents

the capitalized value of the enormous sum of 750,000,000 pounds sterling. That will give the house some conception of what is involved in a matter of this kind. From year to year in Great Britain the state finds the sum necessary to take care of that lag until such time as the fund created by the joint contribution of employer and employee with the aid of the state is sufficient to meet the demands that may be made upon it. I hesitate to do so, but in the event of your honour concluding that the resolution is in order I would suggest the following amendment. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) :-
That all words after the word "that" in the fifth line in the said resolution be deleted and the following substituted therefor:-
Whereas there exists in Canada an acute unemployment situation;
And whereas it is desirable that as many as possible be absorbed into the useful industrial life of the dominion;
Therefore be it resolved, that the government be requested' to forthwith take appropriate measures for investigating, considering and determining the extent to which, under existing conditions, useful productive employment may be made available for the unemployed, if employed persons of the age of sixty and over are retired from their employment, and paid an annual pension or allowance during their lifetime, of such amount and on such terms and conditions as may be determined.
That would enable the government, if it thought desirable, to refer this matter to a committee of this house for investigation or inquiry or to take other means that may be thought desirable to that end. I move this amendment with some hesitancy, and I move it only in the event of your honour concluding that the motion is in order.

Parliamentary Rules and Forms, at page 167, under paragraph 562, that-

speechtext:
That decision stands. I think it is an unheard of thing in the house that the Speaker, merely on the suggestion of a very highly placed member, should reverse a decision once given. We have had no opportunity whatever of arguing the point of order. I would point out, that, according to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, in paragraph 558:
Motions advocating public expenditure, or the imposition of a charge, if the motion be framed in sufficiently abstract or general terms, can be entertained, and agreed to by the house.
Resolutions of this nature are permissible because, having no operative effect, no grant is made or burthen imposed by their adoption.
This is a rule which, ever since I have been in parliament, has been observed in matters of this kind. When any specific question or motion involving a grant has come up, of course it has naturally been ruled out of order, but it has been the practice for many years in this chamber for members to make suggestions as to changes in policy, or the adoption of new policies by governments. There is practically no sort of policy which can be thought of which does not directly or indirectly involve some expenditure of funds, and so in these motions we have been particularly careful not to place the burden directly upon the government, but rather to express an opinion of the house. The resolution is so framed that it is merely an expression of opinion by the house. Of course it will not be passed, with the government having so large a majority, but if it were passed it would not be obligatory upon
the government. Again and again we have had instances where much more specific resolutions have been put before the house, and adopted thereby.
In the present instance it is an extraordinary procedure, I submit, when Mr. Speaker, without having had any appeal against his decision, but simply on the suggestion of a member, should completely reverse that decision, and before having declared his reversal of it, give no opportunity whatever for an argument on the point of order. I would rather appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that it is a serious matter-if we are not going to know when we are in order or not in order, and if decisions can so readily be reversed.
As I have been trying to emphasize, the government does not have to carry out the terms of the resolution. I can look back over dozens of resolutions put forward in these very terms, as requests to the government, and those resolutions have been accepted. We have been here two days debating the resolution, and when one member confessedly states he does not want to face the vote then, forsooth, we have to have the decision of the Speaker reversed. I protest against this.

I would quote Campion's Introduction to The Procedure of the House of Commons, page 152, where I find this under the heading Anticipation of Debate:
The anticipation rule, which forbids discussion on a matter standing on the paper being forestalled, is dependent on the same principle as that which forbids the same question being twice raised in the same session. In applying the anticipation rule preference is given to the discussion which leads to the most effective result, and this has established a descending scale of values for discussions-bills, motions, amendments, et cetera. Thus a bill or other order of the day must not be anticipated by (or more shortly "blocks") discussion of a motion, amendment, or subject raised on another motion, such as that for the adjournment of the house. A motion standing on the paper for leave to bring in a bill blocks discussion of a motion (except for the presentation of a bill), amendments, et cetera.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Whereas it is detrimental to the best interests of Canada that there should be in the country groups to whom, because of race or religious beliefs, we do not extend all the right ot citizenship;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should' take the necessary measures to exclude from the country all persons belonging to those groups to whom we do not grant the full rights and privileges of citizenship.
He said: In the uncertainties of the situation I rather hesitate to get up for fear I may find that I am not in order even with this resolution, though I think it is a matter that has been discussed in the house on other occasions. But in spite of that discussion the problem remains pretty much the same. I can assure the house that I gave the whole subject a great deal of thought before putting the motion on the order paper, because I am convinced that it is one that should be considered and it is much better that it should be discussed on the floor of the house where we can, I hope, give it that impartial and serious consideration which we could not do in the heat of an election, on the hustings; where passions and prejudices can be brought into play.
The resolution asks parliament to take immediate measures to exclude from the country persons to whom, because of race

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Maclnnis
or religion, we do not extend all the rights and privileges of citizenship. I realize that even if this were done it would not meet the situation that exists in British Columbia, with which I will try to deal to-night. Of course, when I speak of persons to whom we refuse to extend the rights and privileges of citizenship, asking that they be excluded from the country, I refer to such persons as come here to stay permanently; the resolution does not refer to persons who may come into the country for a stated time.
In British Columbia, unfortunately, there are persons who are deprived of citizenship rights because of racial origin and religious beliefs. In the Franchise Act of 1934 the Doukhobors in British Columbia were deprived of one of the ordinary rights of citizenship, the right to vote. They were denied that right in British Columbia although they still have it in all the other provinces. I do not however wish to deal to-night with the Doukhobor situation, the present government, when in opposition, took a very decided stand, and in my opinion rightly so, against the disfranchisement of Doukhobors in British Columbia, and it is only reasonable to suppose that that discrimination will be removed from the Franchise Act when it comes up for amendment, as I assume it will before the next general election takes place. There are however in British Columbia other racial groups who are in the same position as are the Doukhobors in regard to the rights of citizenship. I do not know what the attitude of the government would be with respect to those groups, but I do know the attitude of some of its supporters. I refer now to persons of oriental origin, Japanese, Chinese and British subjects from India. These people are not allowed to vote in British Columbia, and they are debarred from other rights and privileges because they have not the right of the franchise. I may refer more specifically later on to these other deprivations.
If the number affected by this discrimination were insignificant, if there were only very few of them, I realize that the moral aspect of the matter would be the same; but the practical consequences would not be so important. I think it is unfortunate that this oriental question affects British Columbia more than it does the other provinces. I believe it would be correct to say that the other provinces have no oriental problem; yet the other provinces, through their representation in the house, cannot avoid responsibility for the situation that now exists in British Columbia.

Before I put the case as I see it, I think it would be well to give the house an idea of the situation in that province by indicating the extent of the oriental population. I will deal first with the Chinese. The number of Chinese in the province at the time of the census in 1931 was 27,139; that was not in the dominion as a whole but in British Columbia alone. Now there is an assumption, which has been very assiduously spread, that this population is growing rapidly. So far as the Chinese are concerned, that is not true. According to the statistics I have received from the bureau of statistics the number of Chinese births since 1931 to the end of 1934 was 488. The number of deaths in the same period was 693, and there has been no Chinese immigration, that is, at least no legal entry of Chinese during the last few years. We can see that the Chinese population is decreasing rather than increasing. The natural decrease for the period I have mentioned would be about 200, and I am told that there are quite a number of adult Chinese who have returned to their native land during the period. There are however no accurate statistics with regard to this category.
When we take the Japanese into consideration the situation is different; the population is growing. And it is for that reason that I say that even though those who are now coming in by immigration were excluded, as I am asking to have done, the Japanese population would continue to grow. I come now to the figures showing the number and the growth of the Japanese population in the province at the present time. According to the census of 1931, there were 22,205 Japanese in British Columbia. Births from the time of the census to the end of 1934 numbered 2,341. There was an increase by immigration during that period of 618, and the number of deaths in the same period was 503. Deduct the number of deaths from the number of births, and add the increase by immigration, and we find that the Japanese population of British Columbia is larger now by 2,456 than it was at the time the census was taken in 1931. The rate of natural increase, however, is declining. The number of births has been decreasing each year from 1929, as shown by the years for which I have statistics, until 1934. The number of births in 1929 was 842; in 1934 the number was 614. As I have pointed out, however, there has been a substantial increase in the population during the three and a half years for which I have given the figures.

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Maclnnis
The statement was made by one of the Liberal candidates in order to frighten the people of British Columbia that in 28 years the oriental population of that province would be greater than the white population. If that is correct, the situation with which I am dealing is even more serious than I believe it to be. We are adding yearly to the population of Canada by natural increase about 650 Canadian-born children who under present circumstances can never become Canadian citizens. That is true not only of children now born; it is true of those children's children for generations unless we deal with the matter in a better and, I would say, a more British way than we have dealt with it so far. I would quote from a speech made to the house by the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) on June 30, 1934. He was speaking against the exclusion of Doukhobors from the franchise in the present Franchise Act. I am quoting the present Minister of National Defence because I agree with what he said at that time. I believe the stand that he took on that occasion was the right one. This is what he said, as reported in Hansard of that year at page 4530:
The province of British Columbia has punished these men and properly so but it is a pernicious, vicious and iniquitous principle to single out any race by name in any legislation of this country and to deprive them of the franchise because this will affect not only the people there to-day but their descendants
to the third and fourth generation_______ But
here we are to-day as a parliament representing all free peoples within this country, saying that any man because he is a Doukobor is absolutely deprived of the franchise and his sons and daughters and their descendants unto untold generations are also to be disfranchised. That is the most Tory measure I ever heard of in any parliament.
It was pointed out that the reason these Doukhobors were to be deprived of their franchise was that they would not observe the laws of this country. If it is a pernicious, vicious and iniquitous principle to deprive the law-defying Doukhobor of the franchise, how much more so is it so with regard to the law-abiding oriental?
I have a number of other statistics with regard to the Japanese population. Those statistics, however, are taken from a private source; I wish to make that clear. They have been gathered by a survey made by a number of university students of Japanese origin in the province of British Columbia. There are approximately 24,000 Japanese in British Columbia at the present time. Over 11,000 of them are Canadian-bom and are consequently in my opinion Canadian citizens, and 135 of those are Canadian-bom children of
Canadian-born parents. It is also shown by this survey that 3,685 Japanese were attending educational institutions, most of them being in the public schools of the province. It should also be noted that, of the Canadian-bom Japanese of ten years and over, 41i per cent read English only. Even if it were possible, which in my opinion it is not, to return these people to the land of their origin, they would be as much out of place there as if they were Canadian-born children of white parents. Forty-four per cent can read English and Japanese, and 14-3 per cent read Japanese only. From the same survey it appears that only 0-2 per cent of Canadian-born Japanese of ten years and over are illiterate. It would seem that according to these figures literacy among the Japanese in British Columbia is very high indeed. I have given the house those statistics in order that we might have, as far as population can show, a picture of the situation that exists in my province.

speechtext: Would the hon. member be prepared to include Canadian Indians in his proposal? They are law-abiding citizens.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext: Canadian Indians, I believe, come under another classification. I do not think there is any discrimination as regards Canadian Indians when they become citizens within the proper meaning of that term. So long as they are wards of the government I understand that they are not allowed the franchise, but if they leave the reserve I think the franchise is granted to them in the same way as to any other Canadian citizen.' I think those are the regulations, if you like to call them such, with regard to Indians. However, I have no objection to including them in this.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext: May I ask another question then. If my hon. friend classifies Indians as wards of the government, how about those people we are keeping on relief? Are they not also wards of the government? Would he also disfranchise them?
