That is not germane to the point under discussion. The Franchise Act of 1934 specifically allowed those who were receiving relief to vote, though they might otherwise have been excluded from the franchise. I agree with the principle, and if I had my way I would extend it much further. However it is not germane to the question I am discussing.
The question may very properly be asked, I believe, as to the way in which this
376	COMMONS
Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Maclnnis
relatively small racial group constitutes a problem that should be discussed in the house. That question can be answered definitely and clearly by saying that these people, citizens of Canada, are deprived of the right to vote, and that they are thus segregated from the rest of the population of British Columbia. They feel that they are in an inferior position; they feel that they should not be placed in this position, as intellectually and in every other way they are the equal of other races or national groups. Recent history has given ample proof of the dangers of discriminating against racial minorities. Canada has prided itself on the fact that there is no racial discrimination in this country. I am told, and I think I saw it somewhere in the press, that our representative at Geneva-and if my memory serves me aright it was the government leader in the other house-recently said that in Canada we had no racial problems. I am afraid that before making that statement the hon. gentleman did not see the advertisements of the Liberal party in British Columbia during the recent campaign; I am afraid he did not listen to some of the radio broadcasts dealing with racial problems in that province. I am quite satisfied that if he had done so he would not have made the statement he is supposed to have made. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is anxious to promote friendly relations between this country and the rest of the world and also that he is anxious that we should not have racial prejudices and racial antagonisms created within this country. For that reason I wish him to note the advertisement to which I am going to refer now, and which appeared in Vancouver newspapers during the last federal campaign. This advertisement appeared in the Vancouver Province of October 7, and it states at the bottom of the page that it is published by the Vancouver Liberal council executive committee. At the top in black type one inch deep or perhaps more it says:
50,000	Orientals in British Columbia
C.C.F. stands pledged to give them the vote. The Liberal party is opposed to giving these orientals the vote. Where will you stand on election day?
The deciding issue in British Columbia was your attitude towards the orientals, whether or not you were going to give them the vote. I should like to impress upon the Prime Minister that it was stated as the policy of the Liberal party that they were opposed to giving the vote to orientals, that they were opposed to giving the vote to these British

subjects, these Canadian citizens, because of the colour of their skin. Then they go on:
A vote for any C.C.F. candidate is a vote to give the Chinaman and Japanese the same voting right that you have! A vote for a Liberal candidate is a vote against oriental enfranchisement.
When the Japanese were members of the League of Nations did not they and the Chinese have in that body the same voting right that any other nation possessed? That was in the League of Nations, the greatest body of its kind this world has ever known. There they stood, the equals of all the other nations in the world, yet the Liberal party in British Columbia felt the need of securing votes so desperately that they had to appeal to low racial prejudices of that kind in order to secure election. I think that is a most unworthy motive. I am sure that there was enough, even if I do not agree with it, in the platform of the Liberal party to secure their election without making appeals of this kind. I wish to suggest to the Prime Minister that at some future time this sort of thing may create a very serious situation in Canada. As I have already pointed out, the oriental population is growing. They are an intellectual, proud people and they will not tolerate reflections of this kind without a protest.
This advertisement is flanked on either side by pictures of the six Liberal candidates in greater Vancouver. Here we have the picture of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). There is a short biography under each picture. I am not going to take the time of the house to read them, except to note that the Minister of National Defence is said to be a national figure and the right bower of the Prime Minister. I am sorry that the right bower of the Prime Minister had to stoop to something like this in order to secure election. Then there is the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), the Liberal candidate for Vancouver East and the Liberal candidate for Vancouver South, who has since been made a judge. I am just wondering what may happen if he has to deal with matters concerning both whites and orientals. Here is the picture of the Liberal candidate for Vancouver North, and the picture of the Liberal member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). In another advertisement directly below we find the picture of the Minister of National Defence again, along with that of an assistant speaker, Mrs. Nellie McClung, the noted author. I understand, however, that Mrs. McClung did not help their election, at least as far as this

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Maclnnis
slogan was concerned, because she put herself on record as being in favour of extending the vote to orientals. I am sure that is very much to her credit.
I could show the house other advertisements of a similar kind. The whole issue was: where will you stand on election day? The determining factor was the stand on the oriental question. Of itself that would not be quite so bad. But it was not left at that. I have in my hand now a radio address delivered on October 4 by a man named J. Edward Sears, barrister at law, which was published by the Vancouver East Liberal campaign committee. Let me quote from this. Do hon. members who are living side by side with other races in eastern Canada, French and English, think this is likely to promote racial accord in British Columbia?
Maybe you have asked yourself. Why has the C.C.F. promised votes to the orientals? It certainly did not emanate from the ordinary white citizen of the province.
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members apparently are not ordinary white citizens.
Is it love of country that has prompted such a promise? Is it personal love for the oriental that has caused the promise of the gift of the franchise? Or is it because the orientals have paid for the promise of such a gift from the C.C.F. ? That is the question that I dare the C.C.F. leaders to answer.
I did not think the franchise was a gift; I thought for British subjects and Canadian citizens it was a right, and consequently people did not have to pay in order to get it. Then comes one of the filthiest things to which anyone could possibly stoop. It goes on to say:
White girls procured for orientals.
You mothers of young girls, wake up, when some one asks you to vote for a C.C.F. candidate in this election. Look behind the solicitor for a C.C.F. candidate and you will see an oriental leering over his shoulder with an eye on you and your daughter. Remember the terrible evidence that came out during the trial of the men of foreign extraction a few months ago, who procured and drugged innocent young girls and forced them into a life of shame.
Can hon. members imagine a great party stooping to a thing like that? It is true that trials were held and certain people were convicted and sent to the penitentiary. But they were not orientals; they were other Canadian citizens of foreign extraction who have the rights of citizenship. And in any event what did we do in this country? We brought thousands of Chinese men here; we kept them here; we did not permit their wives and families to come with them, and we should have known that Canadian women and girls would have
to pay for an immoral act of that kind. Now it is time that something should be done to rectify such a situation, but surely the way to do it is not to make these low appeals to racial prejudice.
May I also point out that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is not the only organization in British Columbia that has gone on record in favour of giving the vote to orientals. The United Church of Canada in British Columbia has gone on record to the same effect. I wonder whether those members of the Liberal party when they went to their churches on Sunday and the minister preached to them, would see an oriental leering over his shoulder with an eye on their wives and daughters. I wonder I I quote again from this thing, although I am sure I have quoted enough:
Mr. Woodsw'orth, the leader of the C.C.F. party in Canada, had the effrontery and heathenism to announce in the Canadian parliament on the 22nd day of June last year that it was the policy of the C.C.F. party to grant the franchise to the orientals of this province and he gloried in it.
Well, he will be glad to find that at least he is in good company as far as his heathenism is concerned, because he is here associated with the United Church of Canada, and also with the Women's Christian Temperance Union, some more heathens I suppose!
Here is another one, very typically Liberal I believe:
C.C.F. would have orientals elect candidates.
I want you to stop and think what might happen in a few years if the oriental is given the vote. Maybe you want a small concession from the government, a job, or a small contract of some kind, or a piece of land-
How typically Liberal!
-or to have your child given a little special attention _at school. It is necessary to make a trip to Victoria and see the minister directly concerned. You go into his office in the parliament buildings and you see three or four orientals in the anteroom waiting. Finally you are ushered into the presence of the minister and find yourself gazing into the eyes of a yellow man. You state your business and are then politely told that the others waiting in the outer office are also asking for the same concession. What would be your chance of obtaining any help?
I will not quote any more from the vile thing. But that is what we have to contend with in British Columbia. I think I have shown sufficiently where we are heading if this appeal to race prejudice is going to continue. We know how easily clashes can be brought about by such appeals. As I have already pointed out, the oriental population in British Columbia will keep on increasing for a considerable number of years. As I have also
378	COMMONS
Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Maclnnis
pointed out, the orientals are an intelligent and proud people and they will not forever put up with vilification and abuse of the kind I have just read.
What I would like to put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is this: First, I ask that the agreement between the Canadian government and the government of Japan by which a certain number of Japanese come to this country each year should be terminated at the earliest possible date. If the Japanese cannot be given full rights of citizenship in this country then we certainly should not allow any more of them to come into Canada. We also should take steps to return to the land of their origin as many as possible of those who are here. But this in itself would not be a solution of the problem. The orientals are in our midst; why they are here, who brought them here I am not going to discuss to-night. The important point is that they are here, and as far as I can see they are here to stay. It would be very much more to the point, now that they are here, to do everything possible to make them good and loyal citizens, having pride in our institutions, than because of their colour to try to create race prejudice against them in the minds of the ignorant.
Speaking recently to the advertising bureau, I think it was, of the board of trade of Vancouver, Professor Angus of the university of British Columbia made this statement. He had pointed out that there was no possible practical alternative, so far as our oriental population was concerned, to giving them the franchise. Then he said:
It is the best thing to do from the selfish interests of us who are not oriental. We have to live with them, and it is much better to live with good citizens than bad citizens.
Some little time ago I was talking to a principal of one of the Vancouver schools at which there is an attendance of children of, as he told me, twenty-eight different races. He stated that there was no difficulty whatever, so far as racial grounds were concerned. The children played together; they worked together and so far as he could see race made no difference. My home in Vancouver is near one of the Vancouver high schools, and any day one can walk along the street and see Japanese girls accompanied by white girls, or Chinese girls and white girls walking arm in arm along the sidewalk. The same is true of the university.
Quite recently a farmer from the Fraser valley came to my home to talk over with
me the necessity for the exclusion of orientals. During the interview he made this amazing statement:	"It is not the vices of the

orientals to which we object; it is their virtues." By a proper approach to this question I believe the government of Canada could turn the virtues of our oriental citizens to good account, and I implore the Prime Minister, in whose sincerity on questions of this kind I have the greatest trust, to try to find some way of dealing with the matter. I am not asking that at the moment the franchise be extended to orientals, but I am asking that if it is not extended some other solution of the problem be found.
With the statement of Professor Angus I am in complete accord. As these orientals are in Canada I think it is much better that we try to make good citizens of them because it is better to live with good citizens than with bad. I believe the time at my disposal has expired. I trust that any hon. member speaking on the resolution will endeavour to see the situation as it affects British Columbia. This matter does not affect other provinces to the same extent, but I believe it cannot be settled without the assistance of the dominion as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been following with great care the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). May I say to him immediately what he has been kind enough to say to me, namely, that I greatly respect his sincerity in everything he has said.
In listening to the hon. member however I found some difficulty in understanding his real objective. As I listened to his observations it seemed to me that they were directed towards the advocacy of the franchise being given to certain orientals in the province of British Columbia. I find however that the operative portion of his resolution asks the house to do something wholly different, and I believe it important to bring that difference to the attention of hon. members immediately, so that if the debate goes on for some time, hon. members will not be confused with respect to the real issue in the resolution as drafted.
May I point out that the resolution is divisible into two parts, the first constituting the preamble and the second the operative portion. The preamble reads:
Whereas it is detrimental to the best interests of Canada that there should be in the country groups to whom, because of race or religious beliefs, we do not extend all the rights of citizenship.
Hon. members will notice that the preamble relates entirely to citizenship, a question

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Mackenzie King
which is wholly domestic. It is intended to deal with that phase of citizenship which the hon. member has emphasized, namely the right of the exercise of the franchise.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext: Without unduly interrupting the right hon. gentleman may I state I pointed out clearly that while I was anxious to exclude all those to whom we could not extend the rights of citizenship I felt that would not be a full solution of the problem which now exists.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
I now come to the operative portion of the hon. member's motion:
Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should take the necessary measures to exclude from the country all persons belonging to those groups to whom we do not grant the full rights and privileges of citizenship.
That portion of the resolution makes it one for the exclusion of orientals. That is what it is, and my hon. friend agrees. We are perfectly clear on that point; as a consequence, I believe there will be very little difficulty in deciding the proper course for parliament to follow.
I agree with the hon. member when he states that questions of this kind can be discussed to much greater advantage in a deliberate assembly, such as the House of Commons, than on the hustings, and I am therefore glad the hon. member has brought the matter here for discussion. May I revert to the preamble, which deals impliedly with the question of the franchise, and say that if it is a question of granting the franchise to orientals resident in British Columbia, the province to which he has made particular reference, then the matter is one which it seems to me might come properly before the legislature of that province, in the first instance, and might come properly before this chamber during the consideration of our Dominion Franchise Act. If I am not mistaken, the party to which the hon. member belongs constitutes the opposition in the legislature of British Columbia, but I am not aware that the co-operative commonwealth federation party in the legislature has preferred any request to the government of British Columbia to give the right of the franchise to the orientals of that province. I would say that that would be the proper place to begin. As long as I can remember, with respect to the franchise, we in the federal parliament have felt it our duty to respect the points of view of the provinces in matters of this kind.

There are
exceptions to every rule, and I am quite prepared to grant my hon. friend the exception. But certainly so far as orientals in British Columbia are concerned, any portion of our legislation respecting the franchise which touches on that question has been dealt with in parliament out of respect for what we believed to be the wishes of the people of that province. However may I state immediately in this connection that there is on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) a notice of motion reading as follows:
That a special committee, the members thereof to be selected at a later date, be appointed to study the Dominion Elections Act 1934 and amendments thereto and the franchise act 1934 and amendments thereto and' to suggest to the house such amendments to the said acts as they may deem advisable, and, furthermore, such committee shall study and make a report on the following subjects:-*
And so on.
I have no doubt that the house will adopt that motion and that the Franchise Act will come before the special committee, and there would seem to me to be the proper time and place for my hon. friend to present his proposal that orientals in British Columbia should be granted the franchise. So far as his motion has to do with the franchise in its relation to orientals, the two courses I have mentioned amply cover all that could possibly be desired with regard to settling a domestic question pertaining to citizenship and the exercise of the franchise by orientals in British Columbia, namely, to have it dealt with in the first instance in the provincial legislature of British Columbia, and in the second place dealt with here by a committee of this House of Commons appointed specially to consider what amendments to the Dominion Franchise Act may be necessary.
May I say just in passing that I am not aware so far as British Columbia is concerned that the orientals themselves who reside there have been agitating for this right of the franchise, nor am I aware that the public generally have been advocating that particular step. However, I mention that only in passing.

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Mackenzie King
The important point to consider is what my hon. friend actually proposes in his resolution, and here I think I can almost quote him in support of the point of view that I am about to set forth. The substantive portion of the resolution, as I have mentioned, is:
That the government should take the necessary measures to exclude from the country all persons belonging to those groups to whom we do not grant the full rights and privileges of citizenship.
The groups referred to, as mentioned by my hon. friend, are four: the Doukhobors, the Japanese, the Chinese and the Hindus.
My hon. friend says that so far as the Doukhobors are concerned, they have not been coming to this country for a long time past and therefore the question of excluding them does not arise.
My hon. friend also mentioned one other point, which was that members on the government side of the house at the present time opposed very strongly the denial in the Dominion Franchise Act of the right of the exercise of the franchise to Doukhobors residing in the province of British Columbia. I know that I opposed that provision very strongly at the time, and I am opposed to that section as it stands at present. I have no doubt that particular clause will come before the committee for consideration. So as far as the Doukhobors are concerned, they can be ruled out of the present discussion altogether.
The Chinese, I heard my hon. friend say, were diminishing rather than increasing in numbers in Canada, and from that point of view it would seem that exclusion of Chinese was hardly a step that it would be wise for this country to take at the present time even if there were not other very strong reasons for not taking action of that sort.
My hon. friend did not make quite clear just what he meant by exclusion, whether he meant to take the orientals already in the country and have them removed bodily back to their own native land, or whether he wished to exclude others from coming in. I think he did say that he thought they could hardly be sent back. He did not make the statement too positively, but he did think it would not do to send them back. I think I am right in saying that such at any rate is his view. If that, then, is the case, what the resolution narrows down to is simply the exclusion of others from coming in. We are agreed on that. So far as the Doukhobors are concerned we have seen that the resolution has no bearing as they have not been coming in. As far as the Chinese are con-

cerned, the hon. member himself, as I have pointed out, states that their numbers in the province are diminishing, and he admits that none have come in at all within the last couple of years; so exclusion there would not be very much to the point. There remain then but the two nationalities, the Japanese and the Hindus-the British East Indians, spoken of colloquially as the Hindus. That raises, Mr. Speaker, the very large question of the exclusion from our dominion of some of those who are British subjects and also the exclusion of citizens of a great friendly power such as Japan is. These are days .when the world is severely troubled with its problems. I should think it very unlikely that hon. members would wish to add to the world's problems to-day by raising at this time the question of exclusion from this country of the foreign peoples of the orient and of British subjects from India. I cannot imagine a single question which at this time would create more difficulties to governments, and which was calculated to provoke more in the way of hatred and strife than the proposal of exclusion.

speechtext:
May I say
to my hon. friend that this is a question which has caused all governments in Canada for many years past great concern. It is a question to which I personally have given a good deal of attention and investigation. I have in my hand a report which I prepared for the government of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier as long ago as the year 1908 after a mission to England to confer with the British authorities on the subject of immigration to Canada from the orient, and immigration from India in particular. Having taken up outstanding features of this problem, so far as Canada was concerned, with the British Government, I subsequently visited India and took the matter up with the government of India. Later on I took up the same question with the governments of China and Japan. I have had much to do with subsequent negotiations. So I think I can speak with some degree of authority as to the significance of this great question. May I be permitted to quote just one paragraph of the order in council under which I was appointed to go to England to discuss the matter with the British government and subsequently to India. It is as follows:
That moreover the whole subject of oriental immigration is one of first concern to Canada, and affecting, as it does, the relations of the dominion with foreign powers, and the relations of our people with fellow British subjects in India, involves considerations of the highest importance, not only to Canada, but to the British empire as a whole.
That was greatly true in 1908. Some twenty-eight years have elapsed since that time. I venture to say the problem has become infinitely more significant in its world aspects in that interval of time. It behooves this House of Commons to move very warily and carefully in whatever it does that might be interpreted by the great peoples of the orient and of India as something that is offensive to them as a people, and which reflects upon them as nations.
My hon. friend in speaking to-night said that the orientals as he knew them were a proud people; that they did not like the reflection on their race and their country involved in their being deprived of the franchise and were offended by it. I think he is right in regarding them as sensitive and proud, and just because I think he is right in that I feel we have to be very careful as to anything we say or do in this House of Commons which will be regarded as a reflection and as offensive,
not merely to the few orientals who happen to be in Canada, but to the peoples of the orient in their respective countries whether they be in Japan or China or India or other parts of the world.
That is why I have thought it advisable to intervene at an early stage in this debate rather than to wait for the discussion to run on for some time. As, I said, speaking in the house some days ago, I do not believe that those of us who are members of legislative bodies can begin to appreciate the possible significance of our words and above all of our resolutions at a time like the present, when the feeling of unrest among the nations of the world is what it is. This is one resolution which for this reason I trust the House of Commons, if it should come to a vote at all, will vote down in the most emphatic way. 1 have not the least doubt however that my hon. friend, when he has discussed the political issues of the last campaign in British Columbia, will feel that his purpose has been served and will withdraw the resolution.
May I point out that, the question being the important one it is, every government that has held office in this country has had to give very careful consideration to the best method of dealing with it. There are only two methods that can be adopted with respect to immigration from the orient to Canada. One is the method of exclusion, which reflects upon the entire peoples of those countries, which is offensive to them and which is certain to create bitterness as between the orient and Canada, and the other method is that of diplomatic negotiation-frank and direct communication with the countries concerned, pointing out aspects of the problem as they are of concern to us, and seeking by negotiation in a diplomatic way to effect arrangements which will achieve what is necessary by way of effective restriction and avoid what is so objectionable in exclusion.
The governments that have been in office in this country for thirty years past, whether Liberal or Conservative, have followed precisely the same method in dealing with this question; they have met those in authority in the other countries and explained the situation here, and have succeeded in securing arrangements in the nature of effective restriction. What my hon. friend has said to-night makes it clear that while there have been times when the number of orientals coming to Canada has been considerable, there has never been a time when the numbers coming in have been fewer actually than they are at present. So far as immigration from the orient is concerned, my hon. friend has chosen,

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Mackenzie King
from his point of view, the worst possible moment to introduce a resolution looking in the direction of restriction, to say nothing of exclusion. One of the chief reasons this country had for opening a legation in Japan was that we might avoid precisely the sort of discussion that threatens to arise in the house to-night in considering a question which means so very much to nations that are sensitive in matters of this kind. It was thought that if Canada had a legation in Japan and Japan a legation here, we could meet the representatives of Japan here and the Japanese could meet our representative in Tokyo and these matters could be talked over and a friendly arrangement reached. That has been done and done most successfully. The agreement we have with Japan at the present time is being carried out very faithfully by the Japanese. We have no reason to complain at all of the honourable manner in which that country has acted in the last few years with respect to the fulfilment of all the obligations arising out of the arrangement we have with her.
Again, so far as India is concerned, I should think it would be very unfortunate indeed if we attempted anything in the nature of exclusion. I think my hon. friend himself will agree that the number of East Indians coming to Canada at the present time is so small as not to make it a consideration; indeed, the hon. gentleman's remarks have been pretty much to that effect. So that the whole matter narrow's to the adoption of an act of exclusion towards Japan.
May I say to my hon. friend, that quite apart from the more serious and important considerations of which I have spoken, interested as he is above all in his own province of British Columbia, he surely must appreciate the importance to British Columbia in the development of its trade on the Pacific, of maintaining the friendliest relations with the countries with which Canada hopes to trade.	Within the last few
months, we have fortunately settled a trade difference between Japan and Canada in a manner which has avoided much bitterness of feeling, indeed has, I believe, ended it, and established in its stead friendliness and good will that will be very much to the advantage of both countries. Certainly, in the little time that normal trade relations have been restored, there has been evidence as a result thereof, of a very considerable development of industry in British Columbia. Many men are to-day employed who only a few months ago were out of work; wage

bills are being paid out at higher rates and more extensively in several of the industries in British Columbia as a result of restored trade with Japan. That is a development that means very much to our country at this time, and will mean more and more as time goes on. Any act of exclusion against orientals would pretty soon put an end to trade relations with countries against which that act might be directed.
I do not think I need say more. I believe that my hon. friend is truly desirous, as are all members of the house, of promoting good will as between the different nations of the world and this dominion; and particularly desirous are those who come from British Columbia and from the western part of Canada, of promoting the friendliest relations with those great countries that are across the Pacific. We shall be making no mistake if we continue by direct negotiation to seek to appeal to what is reasonable in the minds of others in effecting the agreements that are necessary to the succesful and peaceful management of our own affairs; but we shall certainly be creating ill-will, the consequence of which no one can foresee, if we adopt at this time any act of exclusion.
May I add this word in conclusion. I do not think that any country would for one moment take the view that immigration is not entirely a matter for each country to settle for itself. So far as the British empire is concerned, at the imperial war conference of 1918, if I am not mistaken, a resolution in quite definite terms was passed to the effect that as between different parts of the empire it was recognized that each part had sovereign right in the matter of regulating the entrance of people into its own domain and that this carried with it the right to restrict immigration from any other part of the empire. As regards our recognized right to do as we please with respect to immigration there can be no question whatever. But what it is best to do, and how it can best be done is something which no government can consider too carefully. I hope therefore that, having served his purpose in bringing out what he regards as deplorable features of the last campaign in British Columbia, my hon. friend will, when the time comes, withdraw the resolution, so that there may be no possible misinterpretation of Canada's attitude towards orientals, whether they be foreigners in the usual meaning of the term, or fellow British subjects in the wide sense of that phrase.

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Reid

subtopic: MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
The resolution now before the house deals with a matter, as the mover (Mr. Maclnnis) stated, peculiar to British Columbia. I was rather disappointed-and I say this kindly- that the mover of the resolution, although he started off upon a rather high plane, remarking that this was a question which should be discussed in the House of Commons, and without heat, rather than on the hustings, before long exhibited quite a little heat and brought in matters that occurred during the last election.
Let me say at the outset that perhaps no Liberal candidate can wholly disclaim the propaganda and advertisements which appeared in the press on behalf of his party. I am not adopting a " holier than thou " attitude, but I can assure the mover of the resolution that from one end of the campaign to the other never by word or inference did I mention the oriental issue. It is true that my picture and my name appeared in the newspaper exhibited, but I think in fairness my hon. friend will have to admit that I, although having nothing personally to do with it, must I suppose accept some responsibility. I am however actually no more responsible for it than he is for every speech that was uttered by every Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member throughout the campaign. In bringing up the matter as one that affects the best interests of Canada, the hon. member shows the house, and rightly so, that it is of vital concern and interest to the people of British Columbia particularly.
The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated the matter very clearly, I think, when he pointed out that the federal parliament was merely carrying out the wishes of the British Columbia government. What annoyed many people in British Columbia and some British Columbia members of the house was that during the last provincial election in that province the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidates, knowing that it was an acute question, and a touchy one, invariably ducked the oriental question when they were asked about it. When the subject of the Doukhobors came up in the house the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) came out with a straightforward statement to the house and to the country that so far as he personally was concerned and his party likewise they, if elected to power, would give the orientals in British Columbia the vote.
Coming to the resolution itself, however, it is threefold. The first part I certainly do not agree with. It says
Whereas it is detrimental to the best interests of Canada that there should be in the country groups to whom, because of race or religious beliefs, we do not extend the rights of citizenship.
Again, to quote the words of the Prime Minister this evening, there are many groups in British Columbia who are being denied the vote who are not as much concerned about it as is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I have met many Chinese; I have met many Japanese and Hindus. Let me say frankly that they are more concerned with making a livelihood, and so long as they can make a little money in British Columbia the vote does not interest them very much. Yet we have members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation who seem to be losing a lot of sleep over oriental groups in British Columbia who have not the franchise.
It is my desire to keep the discussion on a fairly high plane. First, however, I want to make some remarks regarding immigration into this country and some of the races which have been mentioned. The mover referred to Japanese, Chinese and Hindus. I think I am stating the matter fairly when I say that if there is any race that has a grievance against Canada it is those who came to this land from China. In looking up records I find that this race have contributed a total of 813,000,000 to the treasury of this country for their admittance to make a Living. I would also draw to the attention of the house that they are the only race which has a special act designed for their control. None of them, generally speaking, is admitted unless he comes under what is known as the Chinese Immigration Act. In view of the opening up of the orient and particularly of that great country, China, I think this is a matter of which serious notice should be taken. It is not that I am advocating the taking down of the barriers, because I quite agree we have had enough of these orientals, and I would like to see many more of them going back; for as has been pointed out, Chinese in large numbers have been returning to their own country. If my memory serves me correctly, many hundreds, if not a thousand or two, were taken back last year in accordance with some understanding with the Chinese government. Napoleon said, referring to that large country, China, "She sleeps, and it is well." But with her teeming millions beginning to awake I think it is about time we took serious note of the present discrimina-
Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Reid

tion; and if we are going to bar Chinese altogether, let us bar all orientals. Of course at the moment I am not going into that matter, nor am I now advocating such a step much as I would like to. But I say it is very unfair that this one country should have legislation specially designed against any one nation in the orient and then, by some agreement with a nation living alongside, allow that country's nationals into Canada.
I could have wished that the mover of the resolution in his remarks had spoken about the unassimilable races. Let me point out to hon. members that there is more behind this matter than mere voting power or the economic life of people in this country from the orient and from India. My personal view is that we should view very carefully if not with alarm the presence of thousands of an unassimilable race, and until the time comes when we either marry them or they marry amongst our people and begin to assimilate, I think we should go very carefully indeed before granting them too many rights and privileges. In saying that I am giving my own personal views.
In view again of the statement of my hon. friend who moved the resolution that he wished to keep the discussion on a high plane, I wonder that he did not draw the attention of the house to the fact that even the gentleman's agreement with Japan is a little one-sided. At any rate that is my view. We allow their nationals, also Chinese and Hindus, to come into this country, to own land, to make a living and to go about their economic and everyday life without let or hindrance. It is hardly necessary to point out that these groups in various phases of our economic life have been the means of keeping wages lower than they should have been. Again, in Japan, I understand, no one has the right to own land or to vote. So Canada's refusal to grant them just the vote is not wholly one-sided. Japan has made no effort to allow any foreigner to own land within her borders, and I say that when any new agreement is negotiated that fact should be laid before the Japanese government and a little fair play asked from them before her nationals demand too much from us. I doubt however whether the Japanese in Canada are demanding the vote in very large numbers. It is true that one or two students have gone around saying it is an insult to the race that they are not allowed to vote, but taking it by and large I think I am making a correct statement that they are not so much concerned with the vote as they are with making a living in this country. I think it also fair to state that so far as their standards of living are

concerned they are making a wonderfully fine living, in the province of British Columbia at least.
I note that many orientals, when they start in business, are very loath to engage Canadian help if at all, though Canadian industries, paying the same wages in many kinds of work, give them every preference in employment. Japanese concerns in British Columbia, either logging or fishing, do not hire one Canadian, and that is a very serious problem, which we view with some alarm. We see them encroaching on our fisheries, our farms and our forests, and now the statement is made in the press that Japan is getting tired of buying lumber from Canadian lumbermen and is beginning to acquire large tracts of forest land in British Columbia. I venture to state that if they do so not one Canadian will be given employment there; all the workmen will be Japanese, born either in' Canada or in Japan.
Under the old act Japanese born in this country could renounce their citizenship only with the consent of their own country. No one knows how many have done so, but under the new law Japanese can retain their citizenship by simply registering with the Japanese consul. I have no inclination to quarrel with them for not giving up their citizenship; it is their birthright; but why pretend that all Japanese in Canada, either born here or coming from Japan, are entirely British subjects or Canadians? We have no real data as to whether they belong to Japan or whether they are really Canadians.
The Doukhobor question was an entirely different matter. When it came up in the house I voted against the Doukhobor being given the franchise, and I am not apologizing for having done so. As is well known, the Doukhobors came to this country-after having been given every encouragement, it is true-and were allowed to live their own lives and go their own way. But when they refused to be registered; when they burned down our schools; when they tore the clothes off the policemen who went in to administer the law, and chased them; when, as the Prime Minister pointed out, they became the first race in this country successfully to defy the law, I have no apology to offer for voting against those people being permitted the franchise until they learn to obey our laws. The extent to which naturalization will confer privileges has varied both in this country and elsewhere.

that of naturalization. A great many of these orientals are naturalized. Certain regulations are laid down. They have to know one of the two languages, and so on. Among the white people are we going to exclude all those who did not go to the front? We do not do that. Further, the sons and daughters of the men who fell at the front are not given the rights of citizenship. We have a monument to those who fell; we give the franchise to those who came back, but we refuse the rights of citizenship to their sons and daughters. Is that how a grateful country treats those who have been willing to lay down their lives for their country?
I have visited several times one of those schools in Vancouver in which there are many oriental children. I was there last Christmas. I listened to their program of Christmas carols and patriotic songs. The principal said to me on one of my visits as we looked over the large number of bright Chinese and Japanese boys and girls, "Mr. Woodsworth, when are you people at Ottawa going to give these young people the vote?" Some people say that the orientals are more interested in the right to live than in the right to the franchise. That may be true, but the unfortunate part is that the refusal to give them the right to vote restricts greatly their opportunity to earn a living. Is it nothing in itself that a man should have the right to vote? We were told that the Boer war was fought very largely because Englishmen did not have the fullest privileges of citizenship in South Africa. Yet we are denying to certain people in this country the full rights of citizenship. I am thinking particularly of these second generation Japanese, people who were born in this country. Half of them cannot read Japanese; most of them can talk Japanese more or less, but they cannot read Japanese. They are brought up in our schools, sing our Christmas songs, go through our patriotic exercises, and

yet when they grow up they cannot vote. They attend our high schools and universities. They are absolutely cut off from Japan. I remember being in Japan just about a year ago and meeting some American and Canadian-born Japanese who had gone back to Japan with their parents. They were like fish out of water in Japan. There was no place there for them. They were Canadians and Americans. These young people do not want to go to Japan because there is no place there for them. They say that this is their country; they think they ought to have the rights of citizenship, and I heartily agree with them.
Just look at what this legislation means. I quote from a summary of an article by Professor H. F. Angus in a publication of the Canadian Institute of International Affairs. He points out that the Revised Statutes of British Columbia of 1924, chapter 76, section 5 (a) disqualifies "any person of Japanese race, naturalized or not," from voting at any election. The effect of this statute which discriminates against oriental Canadians purely on the ground of race does not merely exclude these British subjects of oriental race from voting at municipal, provincial and dominion elections but also restricts them from various fields of occupation by the use of voters lists, provincial or municipal as the case may be, as the basis of qualification. It is by this method that Japanese-British subjects are excluded from:
1.	Election to the provincial legislature;
2.	Nomination for municipal office;
3.	Nomination at an election of school trustees;
4.	Jury service.
Other legislative provisions result in effective exclusion of British subjects of Asiatic race from:
1.	The legal profession;
2.	The pharmaceutical profession;
3.	Obtaining a licence for hand-logging;
4.	Becoming a contractor on any public work;
5.	Purchasing crown timber or logging such timber.
In addition to these statutory and regulatory restrictions against oriental Canadians, there are "de facto" exclusions from:
1.	Being employed as specialists in public service;
2.	Holding municipal offices.
It seems to me a serious matter to allow people to come to this country and compel them to remain in one or two particular kinds of occupation, and I do not know why they should be allowed in these any more

Standing Committees
than in the legal or the medical profession. At any rate, we exclude them in practice from certain higher positions which they are well qualified to fill. I do not think this is fair.
Not only is it unfair to these young Japanese bom in Canada but it is unfair to the Canadian people. Let this continue and what shall we have? We shall have here a subordinate race whose lower standard of living will be a constant menace to the standard of living of other Canadian people. We shall have here a large group of young people educated in our schools, trained in the ideas of democracy but denied absolutely the right to exercise their democracy. Is that a good thing for Canada?
Let me again appeal to Liberal traditions. Surely it is not a good thing to have in our midst a subject race, as well educated as we are, many of them better educated, because the Japanese are not an inferior people- it is not, I say, a good thing for us to have such people here trying to earn a precarious living while excluded from a great many occupations, and with a rankling sense of injustice because they are not granted full rights of British citizenship. I would make this suggestion. All of us have been drawn more or less into political considerations in our discussion to-night. I am not going to lay the blame on anyone but I would make a suggestion that this matter be discussed in a freer atmosphere.

I have just a few
more words to say. We face a real problem The government might refer a matter of this kind to the committee on industrial and international relations to study and report on some possible solution. That could be done without necessarily talking about exclusion or otherwise complicating matters. Let us try to solve this vital Canadian problem.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
